nameStory: The 'bottlenose' dolphin gets its name from its distinctive short, stubby snout that looks remarkably like the neck of an old-fashioned bottle. This chunky nose shape sets it apart from dolphins with longer, more pointed beaks. The 'common' part simply means it's the most widespread and familiar of the bottlenose dolphin species.
description: The Common Bottlenose Dolphin is the friendly, intelligent marine mammal you've seen in movies and aquariums. These sleek, gray dolphins have that famous curved smile and can grow 8-12 feet long, weighing 300-500 pounds. Their smooth, rubbery skin and streamlined bodies make them incredibly graceful swimmers. While they're found in warm oceans worldwide, spotting one in New England waters is a special treat since they're at the northern edge of their range here.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Large dolphin with a robust, torpedo-shaped body and distinctively short, bottle-shaped snout. The dorsal fin is tall and curved, sitting about halfway down the back like a shark's fin but more backward-leaning.

idTips.label: Skin
idTips.description: Smooth, rubbery gray skin that looks almost metallic when wet. Color ranges from light gray to dark charcoal, often lighter on the belly. The skin feels like a wet inner tube if you're lucky enough to touch one.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Highly social, traveling in groups called pods. Known for playful jumping, riding boat wakes, and that characteristic curved smile. Often seen surfacing in rolling arcs, showing the dorsal fin clearly.

idTips.label: Sound
idTips.description: Makes distinctive clicking sounds, whistles, and squeaks that can sometimes be heard above water. Each dolphin has its own signature whistle, like a name.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in deeper offshore waters and occasionally closer to shore near continental shelf edges. Look for them where warm Gulf Stream waters mix with cooler New England seas.

habitat: In New England, Common Bottlenose Dolphins are found in deeper offshore waters, particularly along the continental shelf edge where depths drop from 200 to over 1,000 feet. They prefer areas where the warm Gulf Stream meets cooler northern waters, creating rich feeding zones. Occasionally they venture closer to shore near Cape Cod and the islands during warmer months.

seasonality.spring: May begin appearing in southern New England waters as temperatures warm. Most active during midday when surface waters are warmest.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for sightings off Cape Cod and the islands. Groups may be seen feeding and socializing in deeper waters beyond the continental shelf.
seasonality.fall: Still present in warmer offshore waters, but beginning to move south as surface temperatures drop. Best viewing during calm, warm days.
seasonality.winter: Very rare in New England waters as they follow warmer currents south. Any winter sightings would be exceptional and likely brief.

funFact: Each bottlenose dolphin develops its own unique whistle signature by their first birthday - essentially their own name that other dolphins can recognize and call back to them across miles of ocean, even when they can't see each other.
confusionNotes: Could be confused with pilot whales, but bottlenose dolphins are much smaller, lighter gray, and have that distinctive curved dorsal fin and bottle-shaped snout instead of the pilot whale's bulbous, melon-shaped head.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'bottlenose dolphin' now refers to the entire genus Tursiops, but this common species was the original bottlenose dolphin before scientists discovered there were actually multiple species. What most people picture when they think 'dolphin' is specifically this common bottlenose species.
compareHints: The Common Bottlenose Dolphin is distinguished from its close relative, the Tamanend's Bottlenose Dolphin, primarily by genetics and subtle skull differences that aren't visible in the field. In New England waters, any bottlenose dolphin you see is most likely the common species, as Tamanend's dolphins prefer more southern, coastal waters. Both look nearly identical to casual observers, with the same bottle-shaped snout and gray coloring.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Tamanend's bottlenose dolphins are virtually identical in appearance to common bottlenose dolphins, but they're ecological specialists of shallow coastal waters.
